name: notcurses
why: A character graphics library that pushes terminals to render images, video, and effects far beyond normal expectations.

brief.what_it_is: Notcurses is a C library, with C++-safe headers and Rust, C++, and Python wrappers, for building text user interfaces on modern terminal emulators. Programs draw into stacked rectangular planes (ncplane objects) using 24-bit color, Unicode, and transparency, and the library renders the composed result to the terminal, quantizing color for limited terminals. It can show still images and video, decoded through ffmpeg or OpenImageIO, using character blitters or pixel protocols such as Sixel and Kitty. It installs nine small tools, including ncls (an ls that displays media), ncplayer, notcurses-demo, and nctetris. It is not an X/Open Curses implementation and not a drop-in ncurses replacement.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says Curses assumes the minimum and lets you step up with effort, whereas Notcurses assumes the maximum and steps down by itself when necessary. The stated goal is vivid color, multimedia, thread safety, and full Unicode in terminal apps that ncurses was not designed for.
brief.how_it_works: Each screen cell is resolved by descending the plane stack from the topmost plane until a glyph and foreground/background colors are locked in, then the resulting frame is blitted to the terminal as UTF-8 characters and escape codes. Each plane cell has two alpha bits per color channel (opaque, blend, transparent, or high-contrast) that control how lower planes show through, and glyph choice is independent of alpha. Terminal capabilities come from terminfo plus queries the library sends to the terminal at startup.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the path in this brief. Building from source needs CMake 3.21+ and a C17 compiler, plus terminfo 6.1+ from NCURSES and GNU libunistring 0.9.10+. Optional extras are libgpm, libqrcodegen, FFmpeg libraries, OpenImageIO 2.15+ (requires C++), doctest, and pandoc. Supported runtimes are Linux 2.6+, FreeBSD 11+, DragonFly BSD 5.9+, Windows 10 1093+, and macOS 11.4+. At runtime, TERM must match your terminal and have an up-to-date terminfo entry, or Notcurses refuses to start. LANG should be a generated UTF-8 locale. Optionally set COLORTERM to truecolor or 24bit when the terminal supports 24-bit color but does not advertise it. Docker users are directed to the README's Environment notes section.
brief.standout: It treats pixel graphics as a first-class part of a text UI: one API covers Sixel, the Kitty graphics protocol, and the Linux framebuffer, with several cell-based blitters as fallbacks. Its plane model adds z-order, per-channel alpha, and sprites to a character grid, which is unusual for terminal libraries.
brief.status: unknown. The GitHub README I fetched has no release date or commit date. The dankwiki release table ends at 3.0.0 (2021-12-01), and the README mentions Unicode 16 octant support, which suggests work after that. I did not check the releases or commit history, so I cannot confirm recent activity. The repository has CI badges for Linux, macOS, and Windows.
brief.caveats: Not a drop-in replacement for ncurses, and it expects a current terminfo database and UTF-8 locale. Output quality depends on the terminal and font: the README says Windows Terminal needs particular fonts and settings, and screen and mosh render poorly. The Linux console supports only a limited glyph set. Some features need optional dependencies, and the full multimedia stack is heavy. Direct Mode is substantially slower and less capable than rendered mode. The dankwiki benchmarks date from 2019 and 2021. The README says the tool list includes notcurses-tester, which the Homebrew executables list omits. Source is Apache-2.0.
quotes: Notcurses abandons the X/Open Curses API bundled as part of the Single UNIX Specification.
Notcurses assumes the maximum and steps down (by itself) when necessary.
It's Apache2-licensed in its entirety, as opposed to the drama in several acts that is the NCURSES license

judge.reason: Notcurses makes terminal graphics a real medium, combining layered translucent planes with image and video protocols in a way ordinary TUI libraries do not.

entry.title: Notcurses
entry.tldr: A terminal graphics library that stacks transparent planes of text and pixels, shipped with demos that play video and show images in your terminal.
entry.deeper_look:
Notcurses is a C library for building text interfaces on modern terminal emulators. Programs draw into stacked rectangular planes using 24-bit color, Unicode, and transparency. The library composes them into one frame and writes it out as UTF-8 and escape codes. It also ships a handful of small tools built on it: ncls, an ls that can display media; ncplayer for images and video; nctetris; and a large demo.

The composition model is the interesting part. For each screen cell, the library walks down the plane stack from the top until a glyph and its foreground and background colors are settled. Each color channel carries two alpha bits (opaque, blend, transparent, or high-contrast) that decide how much of the planes below shows through. Glyph choice is independent of alpha, so you get layered, translucent text on a character grid.

Images and video go through ffmpeg or OpenImageIO. They can be drawn with character-cell blitters, or with real pixel protocols such as Sixel and the Kitty graphics protocol, depending on what your terminal supports. The author puts the design this way: "Notcurses assumes the maximum and steps down (by itself) when necessary." Curses, by his account, assumes the minimum and makes you work to go up.

It is deliberately not an ncurses replacement. It abandons the X/Open Curses API, so existing curses programs will not just run on it. Think of it as a different answer to what a terminal program can be, with wrappers for C++, Rust, and Python.
entry.install:
brew install notcurses
# At runtime TERM must match your terminal and have an up-to-date terminfo entry, or Notcurses refuses to start. Use a UTF-8 locale. If your terminal supports 24-bit color but does not advertise it, set COLORTERM=truecolor.

entry.whats_unique: It treats pixel graphics as a first-class part of a text UI. One API covers Sixel, the Kitty protocol, and the Linux framebuffer, with cell-based blitters as fallbacks. Its plane model adds z-order and per-channel alpha to a character grid, which is unusual among terminal libraries.
entry.caveats: Output quality depends heavily on your terminal and font (screen and mosh render poorly), and it is not a drop-in ncurses replacement.
